title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (Npairs = 1000) comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream deterministic validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) are the only mechanisms that could create paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01] and is reported as a descriptive summary; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) is explicitly labeled exploratory/post‑hoc because it was not prespecified. Total hosted model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We report the exact McNemar as the preregistered confirmatory outcome and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, very high baseline validity, validator scope, and shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation promises operational benefits for network operators but also raises safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that degrade correctness for code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates purely downstream validator and single‑repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions so any paired difference is attributable only to validation and permitted repair.
sections.related_work: Empirical and survey work documents frequent hallucinations and prompt sensitivity in LLMs that affect correctness of generated artifacts including code and configurations [1],[2]. Approaches that enforce schema‑aware planning or constrained decoding reduce syntactic and executable errors in structured domains, though many demonstrations come from non‑NetOps domains and require validator fidelity to transfer benefits to networking [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers advocate verifier‑assisted repair, guarded architectures, and governance layers (protocol‑mediated execution, proof‑carrying authorization, auditability) to reduce automation risks; these contributions present prototypes and architectural arguments but typically lack large‑scale production trials [4],[5],[6]. Our study complements this body of work by preregistering a paired comparison that isolates the incremental effect of downstream deterministic validation and an at‑most‑one repair call when the initial candidate is held constant across conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration, design, and interpretive constraints. The study preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was finalized and frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation. Key preregistered elements: confirmatory paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks drawn from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 synthetic corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. The preregistration also specified paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) as a descriptive secondary summary and prespecified missingness and multiplicity treatments. The preregistration SHA256 is recorded in the execution manifest and the preregistration was frozen before model calls.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and consequences. Because generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, both baseline and guarded episodes begin from exactly the same sampled candidate per task. Under this design any paired outcome difference can only arise from deterministic validator decisions and the permitted repair call(s). The experiment therefore does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generation changes (for example, alternative prompts, constrained decoding, or multiple independent samples) because those arms were not executed.

Models, runtime configuration, and validator. The declared provider/model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature=0. Orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family and validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5, a deterministic digital‑twin validator that enforces workflow policies, required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and returns a binary safe‑deploy verdict.

Task corpus, selection, and scoring. Tasks were selected deterministically using the preregistered ordinal rule to produce exactly 1000 unique tasks. Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels (very_hard, extreme). The validator compares parsed candidate command sequences against manifest constraints and archives structured validator traces per episode. Scoring used scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation to produce a binary validity outcome for each episode as required by the paired analysis.

Execution accounting and missingness. The preregistration limited retries and specified how to treat model/API failures. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 2000, failed_episode_count = 0, hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}. The primary analysis used the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' missingness treatment; preregistered sensitivity analyses treating failures as unsafe were available but not required because failed episodes = 0.
sections.results:
Execution and primary paired outcomes. The run completed all preregistered episodes: planned episodes = 2000; completed = 2000; complete_pairs = 1000; failed episodes = 0. Provider audit (deterministic_reconciliation) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005 and repair stage_count = 5 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). The 2×2 paired contingency table is n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005.

Preregistered confirmatory inferential test and preregistered summaries. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 and therefore does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold; preregistered H1 is not supported. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01] and is reported as a descriptive secondary summary. Because the exact McNemar is the preregistered confirmatory analysis we present it as the primary inference; the bootstrap CI and any one‑sided McNemar (one‑sided p = 0.03125) are explicitly labeled descriptive/exploratory and do not overturn the preregistered confirmatory null.

Repair diagnostics. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred. Representative archived episode traces show validator rejections for required_sequence violations or protected_interface touches, a single allowed repair call per episode, and subsequent validator acceptance in repaired episodes. All raw responses, provider call traces, repair traces (where present), and validator traces are archived with the run. Total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5).

Interpretive note on the bootstrap CI and sparse discordant counts. The bootstrap percentile CI excludes zero ([0.001, 0.01]) despite the two‑sided exact McNemar p = 0.0625 because bootstrap percentiles can produce nonzero percentile bounds when discordant counts are extremely sparse; this behavior reflects the discrete sampling distribution of paired differences under near‑unity baseline success and is the reason we treat the bootstrap interval as descriptive only. The small number of discordant pairs (n10+n01 = 5) drives both the discrete McNemar boundary behavior and the bootstrap sensitivity.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory hierarchy and power reconciliation. The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar is the confirmatory test and it did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI and the one‑sided McNemar are descriptive/exploratory summaries; the one‑sided test was not prespecified and is explicitly reported as post‑hoc. The preregistered power plan assumed baseline ≈ 0.60 and targeted an absolute increase of 0.15; the observed baseline (0.995) is far higher, producing very few discordant pairs and substantially reducing sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch between prespecified power assumptions and observed baseline rates limits the ability of the confirmatory test to detect the small observed absolute improvement.

Mechanistic implications within shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because both conditions reuse the same sampled initial candidate, any improvement arises only from downstream deterministic validation and permitted repair(s). The five observed repairs demonstrate that a validator with sufficient coverage can correct certain ordering/sequence violations; however, the low repair count constrains inference about repair efficacy across broader failure classes. Distinguishing whether low repair incidence reflects strong generator correctness for the chosen model/prompt, corpus characteristics, or validator permissiveness requires follow‑ups that vary generation semantics, repair budget, and validator rule sets.

Threats to validity and external generalizability. Construct validity depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5's rule coverage; omitted semantic checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity is strengthened by deterministic seeding, fixed task selection, and no failed episodes, but the shared_initial_candidate design precludes measuring upstream prompting or constrained‑decoding interventions. External validity is limited by the single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task corpus, and a deterministic validator; generalization to heterogeneous vendor/legacy production environments is therefore limited.

Operational implications and preregistered follow‑ups. Artifact‑grounded evidence shows verifier‑guided repair can prevent some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and repair budget. Preregistered follow‑ups supported by the archive: evaluate independent first‑pass generation arms (no shared_initial_candidate) to measure prompt/decoding interventions; sweep repair budgets (0..k repairs) to quantify marginal returns; expand validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity; and include multiple model families with power calculations aligned to plausible baseline failure rates.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total hosted model calls used = 1005. The preregistered exact McNemar is the confirmatory outcome; secondary/descriptive summaries are explicitly labeled as such. These artifact‑grounded results indicate downstream verifier/repair safeguards can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic settings, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. The archived preregistration, manifests, raw outputs, validator traces, and analysis artifacts support reproducibility and preregistered follow‑ups to broaden model diversity, validator coverage, and repair budgets.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
